title: St Matthew Passion, BWV 244
work.title: St Matthew Passion
work.movement: No. 47 (New Bach Edition No. 39). Erbarme dich, mein Gott — aria for alto; a selected highlight from a complete recording, not the complete Passion
work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. The booklet numbers the aria 47 (the Bach-Gesellschaft and BWV numbering) while the Internet Archive and retail track titles number it 39 (the New Bach Edition). The file contains the aria alone: the preceding chorus and recitative ‘Wahrlich, du bist auch einer von denen — Da hub er an’ (booklet No. 46) is the previous track and the chorale ‘Bin ich gleich von dir gewichen’ is the next. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736.
performers.note: The booklet lists Hertha Töpper for the alto arias and Otto Büchner as the violinist. The label of the LP side that carries Nos. 42–53 credits both and does not assign Büchner to a single number; his identification as this aria’s solo violinist rests on that label and on the booklet naming no other violinist. The booklet also names continuo players for the whole Passion (organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl, whom Discogs also lists on continuo cello); which of them play in this aria is not stated, so they are not listed here.
session.date.value: 23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August)
session.date.note: The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958. Which session produced this aria is not stated.
session.place.note: The booklet credit reads ‘München, Herkules-Saal’.
carrier.label.value: Archiv Produktion (Deutsche Grammophon Gesellschaft, History of Music Division)
carrier.label.note: The labels read ‘Archive Production — History of Music Division Deutsche Grammophon Ges.’ and ‘Stereo’.
carrier.catalogue.value: SAPM 198 009/012 (first stereo edition, four LPs); the scanned export pressing carries ARC 73 125–73 128 / SAPM 198 625–628, with this aria on the side labelled ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b
carrier.catalogue.note: First release year is disputed in the sources: the booklet and Wikipedia say 1959 (the booklet reads ‘LPs released/veröffentlicht/paru 1959’ and prints ℗ 1959 Deutsche Grammophon); Discogs and the Internet Archive LP catalogue give 1958, which is the recording year. Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: First stereo edition: fifth programme side of the set (Discogs side E), track E6 (7:44 on the LP); matrix and take numbers not read
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The side and position come from the Discogs tracklist, whose first edition is automatically coupled, so the programme side is not the physical side of a particular LP; the scanned export label for ‘No. 42–53 Trial in the Presence of Kaiphas and Pilate (24’26)’ is numbered 5 (ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b). No run-out inscription was seen, so matrix and take are unknown.
transfer.credits.note: No remastering engineer or studio is credited in the item metadata or the booklet. The booklet’s © 2001 Deutsche Grammophon notice and the retail page’s ‘Digitally remastered’ line show only that commercial digital releases exist. The upload is a private Internet Archive upload in the hifidelity collection.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is established. The Internet Archive item was created on 16 February 2026; that upload date is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: 24-bit/192 kHz FLAC (item description ‘1959 [FLAC 24-192]’), digitally remastered according to the retail page; streamed here through the Internet Archive’s VBR MP3 derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The item’s track titles and durations (7:46 for this track) match the retail page’s 2016 hi-res listing, so the file is probably that release, but the item names no source. No speed correction, noise reduction or restoration settings are stated.
digital.format: Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivative (11,386,076 bytes) of the uploaded 24-bit FLAC (465.67 s); the FLAC itself is over 100 MB and was not downloaded
rights.composition.value: Bach’s composition (d. 1750) and the Bach-Gesellschaft edition used for the orchestra view (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854) are public domain.
rights.composition.note: IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.
rights.recording.value: territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959).
rights.recording.note: Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

title: Concerto for Orchestra, Sz. 116
movement: II. Giuoco delle coppie — Allegretto scherzando
work.title: Concerto for Orchestra
work.version.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
work.version.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.
performers.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.
session.date.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.
session.place.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.
carrier.label.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.
carrier.catalogue.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.
transfer.credits.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.
transfer.date.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.
transfer.processing.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.
digital.format: Internet Archive original MP3; selected file 2.GiuocoDelleCoppie.mp3
rights.composition.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
rights.composition.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
rights.recording.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

performers.note: The item assigns first and second violin; DAHR confirms the four names and instruments. The photographed label uses the spellings Lener, Smilovits, Roth and Hartmann.
session.date.note: These are four session dates for the issued masters, not one continuous performance. AX300–301: 11 February; AX323–328: 21 February; AX332: 22 February; issued AX302 take 4: 25 August. session.place.note: The studio is named by the transfer author on the Archive item. The consulted individual DAHR master records independently give London, not the studio.

carrier.catalogue.note: Five double-sided 12-inch discs. The Archive description dates both British and US publication to November 1924. Movement-to-side allocation comes from the Archive description, with AX301, AX302 and AX332 individually corroborated by DAHR part titles. transfer.credits.note: The description says ‘My transfer’ and identifies the British source discs, but does not name the transfer engineer. The uploader account and shellackophile-recordings collection are not expanded into a personal mastering credit.
transfer.date.note: 27 February 2022 is the item’s added/public date and a digital-file timestamp, not an established date of the analogue transfer.
transfer.processing.value: Ten acoustic-era disc sides joined into one file; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative of an uploaded FLAC.
transfer.processing.note: The item describes the acoustic-era recording and continuous presentation; its file list names the FLAC parent of the selected MP3. The photographed label specifies ‘Speed 80’, not a demonstrated playback speed of this transfer. Stylus, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, join edits, speed adjustment and absolute pitch calibration are unestablished. No tuning value is inferred from automatic key estimates, and no portamento or tempo habit is asserted as an audited feature of this performance.

rights.composition.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel score are public domain.
rights.composition.note: Op. 131 dates from 1826 and was published after Beethoven’s death in 1827. IMSLP identifies the consulted engraving as the 1863 collected edition, plate B.50, and marks it Public Domain. This is not clearance of any unidentified later performing edition.
rights.recording.value: United States public-domain basis: first published in 1924, before the project’s 1926 cutoff.
rights.recording.note: The transfer author expressly dates Columbia L1581–L1585 and US 67021-D–67025-D/Set 6 to November 1924; DAHR corroborates their identity with the 1924 masters, not independently the November publication month. Under the Copyright Office’s stated 95-plus-5-year term for recordings first published in 1923–1946, a 1924 publication has exhausted that term. The Archive metadata supplies no separate Creative Commons recording licence. Admission rests on the historical recording’s US term, not Beethoven’s death, the upload date, an uploader licence or a blanket worldwide clearance. No separate restoration rights claim was identified in the consulted item.

title: String Quartet No. 15 in A minor, Op. 132
work.title: String Quartet No. 15 in A minor
work.movement: III. Molto adagio (Heiliger Dankgesang); the source’s III–IV combined title is disputed
work.version.value: Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed.
work.version.note: The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A-major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.

rights.composition.note: The quartet was composed in 1825; Beethoven died in 1827. The consulted Beethovens Werke engraving, plate B.51, is catalogued as the 1863 edition and Public Domain. This does not clear an unidentified later performing edition or the sleeve author’s prose.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established.
rights.recording.note: The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

movement: II. Adagio — Sehr feierlich und sehr langsam
work.title: Symphony No. 7 in E major
work.movement: II. Adagio — Sehr feierlich und sehr langsam
work.version.note: Neither the Commons page, the IMSLP performance entry, the embedded tags nor the Munich analysis page names the edition performed (Gutmann 1885, Haas, Nowak or Cohrs). The 1885 first edition is cited only as a viewable public-domain score for the orchestration timeline. Whether the cymbal-and-triangle clash at the climax is played is not established from the sources; the audio analysis cannot decide it.
performers.note: The IMSLP performance entry gives “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (Munich), Marcus Bosch (conductor)”, the MP3’s embedded artist tag reads “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (München), Ltg. Marcus Bosch”, and the Munich analysis page repeats the credit. The Commons page credits only “University of Music and Theatre Munich” as author. No roster of players is given.
session.date.value: 2020 (credits) or 8 November 2021 (inferred from file names and a programme listing)
session.date.note: The credits (IMSLP: “Live recording at the University of Music and Theatre Munich 2020”; embedded date tag; Commons; Munich analysis page) give 2020. The IMSLP file names, however, carry the token 2021-11-08, and the Gasteig November 2021 programme lists a Hochschulsymphonieorchester München concert under Marcus Bosch with Bruckner’s Seventh at the Isarphilharmonie, 19:00, under Mo 08. That matching concert is an inferred association, not proof that the files were cut from it; neither date is promoted to a settled session date, and no day or month is documented in the credits.

The Gasteig programme lists a concert with the same forces at the Isarphilharmonie; whether the recording was made there is not established.

title: Piano Trio in G minor, Op. 17
work.title: Piano Trio in G minor
work.version.value: Original scoring for violin, cello and piano
work.version.note: The original label identifies the movement and the three instruments. The session’s edition and part materials are not established. Section timings follow the score and the recording’s broad contrasts; there is no bar-level alignment or listening review.
performers.note: The label names The Mannes-Gimpel-Silva Trio and prints Gimpel’s given name as Bronislav; that spelling is retained.
session.date.note: Jonathan Woolf identifies Clara’s Trio as recorded at the same 1951 sessions as the Beethoven coupling. No precise session date is established. The Archive date field separately describes the LP publication.
session.place.note: The transfer metadata and consulted reissue review do not establish the recording venue. The US release country is not treated as a session location.
carrier.label.note: Original 33⅓-rpm LP label, not the Forgotten Records reissue.
carrier.catalogue.note: Internet Archive dates the LP to 1951. A contemporary review independently establishes commercial publication by September 1952; the rights assessment uses that documented upper bound.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side 1, band 3; printed label matrix MG 2301
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The Andante is the third movement listed on side 1 and the third segmented derivative. MG 2301 is the printed side matrix. No individual take or tape number is established.
transfer.credits.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation
transfer.credits.note: The item belongs to the Boston Public Library vinyl collection. No unverified personal mastering credit is inferred from operator accounts.
transfer.date.note: The ripping_date field is 20210715042255. This is the transfer date; the sleeve and labels were scanned separately in June 2021.
transfer.processing.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; segmented VBR MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The playback and digitisation chain is stated in the item’s lineage field. Equalisation, pitch correction and noise-reduction settings are not documented.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of a mono vinyl LP transfer
rights.composition.value: Public domain under ordinary life-plus-70 terms; the original score was published in 1847 and Clara Schumann died in 1896.
rights.composition.note: This assessment concerns the historical composition and first edition, not an unidentified modern edition or every jurisdiction.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: commercial publication on Decca DL 9555 documented by September 1952, before 1963.
rights.recording.note: The project’s pre-1963 rule relies on expiry of the former 50-year phonogram term before the 2013 extension. Audio Engineering reviews this LP in September 1952. The year 1952 is a conservative publication-by date, distinct from the documented 1951 sessions and the Archive’s 1951 release attribution. US recording status is not established. This is not a Creative Commons licence or worldwide clearance.

title: Les Barricades mystérieuses
work.title: Les Barricades mystérieuses
work.catalogue: Second Livre de pièces de clavecin, Sixième Ordre
work.version.value: Solo piano performance of the harpsichord rondeau
work.version.note: The nominated file contains the individual character piece, not the complete sixth ordre. The work was published in the 1717 second book. Meyer’s performing edition and every repeat choice are unestablished; the inspected modern score is an analytical reference, not an attribution of her edition. No uncut claim is made from duration alone.
performers.note: Commons identifies Meyer; the pianist’s recording chronology identifies the Couperin programme. This is a piano performance, notwithstanding the source category for harpsichord music.
session.date.note: This uncertainty is stated in the Commons Author field. The recording chronology gives the broader 1953/1954 range. No single year or session day has been selected. 23 September 2023 is the Commons upload date, not the session; the filename’s 1954 does not resolve the range.
session.place.note: Venue stated by Commons and the recording chronology; no studio log has been inspected.
carrier.label.note: Named in Commons’ source reference to the Médiathèque musicale Mahler collection and in the recording chronology.
carrier.catalogue.note: Both sources identify DF 86; the chronology identifies an LP issue. No exact first-publication date is inferred from the recording date.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or side identifier securely tied to this transfer is supplied by the opened sources. An earlier Meyer performance is separately listed in the chronology; its 1946 matrix has not been attached to this later file.
transfer.credits.note: Commons names the Médiathèque musicale Mahler collection as source and Flopinot2012 as uploader. Neither attribution establishes the transfer or mastering engineer.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is identified. The upload occurred on 23 September 2023; the MP3 transcoding date is a separate access-file event.
transfer.processing.note: The source upload is FLAC and Commons supplies an MP3 derivative. Equalisation, denoising, speed correction, editing and the equipment used for the transfer are not documented.

title: Flute Concerto in G major, Wq 169 / H 445
work.title: Flute Concerto in G major
work.version.value: Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only
work.version.note: Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.
performers.note: Both sources name the soloist and ensemble. The opened programme does not identify a conductor for this concerto or its continuo player. Credits for soloists in the adjacent Brandenburg concertos have not been transferred to this track. Exact string numbers, keyboard type, double-bass participation and tuning are unestablished.
session.date.note: Commons gives February 2008 and the upstream Music of the Bach Family programme gives 10 and 17 February. The source does not identify which concert supplies this performance or whether material was combined. The directory’s 7 April 2008 file timestamps and Commons’ 23 November 2008 upload are not session dates. MAR-08 is a repository folder name, not proof of a March performance.
session.place.note: The opened recording page, concert programme and notes do not identify the recording venue. The orchestra’s usual location does not establish this session’s place.

session.date.note: The chronology’s BM-C#051 entry gives 28 February 1946 and matrix 2EA10890-1, matching the selected carrier. The source is secondary; no independently accessible DAHR session entry was established. The item’s year 1946 is not itself treated as a day-level session date.
session.place.note: The venue is explicitly named in the matching matrix entry, not inferred from HMV’s address or the performer’s residence.
carrier.label.note: Original British 12-inch 78-rpm disc; Made in England and speed 78 appear on the viewed label.
carrier.catalogue.note: The original label identifies C.3485. Internet Archive assigns the item the catalogue year 1946; the label does not print that date and a contemporary release notice has not been established.

GBIA3042373B is the repository identifier, not a claim that the label prints a B-side designation. No alternative take is substituted; DAHR corroboration remains unavailable.

transfer.date.note: No transfer date is explicitly stated. The 2024 repository public/added dates and file modification times are not promoted to a transfer date.

rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — EU public-domain term basis for a phonogram published before 1963; territorial, not worldwide.
rights.recording.note: The selected HMV C.3485 item is catalogued as published in 1946. That catalogue year, rather than the session date alone, supplies the pre-1963 publication basis. carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Side and band follow the label and segmented filenames. No runout matrix, stamper, session take or original tape number has been established.

transfer.date.note: Derived directly from the item’s ripping_date field, 20201121083807. The 2020-10-21 scan date is a separate event.
transfer.processing.value: Technics SL1200MK5 with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → RDL EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; segmented VBR MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The item documents the playback and digitisation chain. Equalisation settings, pitch correction, noise reduction and further restoration are not established.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of a mono vinyl LP transfer
rights.composition.value: Underlying Debussy composition is out of copyright under ordinary life-plus-70 terms; the original published score is historical.
rights.composition.note: Debussy died in 1918. This is a term assessment of the composition, not a blanket clearance for unidentified modern editions or every jurisdiction.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: lawful commercial publication in 1956, before 1963.
rights.recording.note: The 1956 Mercury mono LP publication predates 1963; under the programme’s rule its former 50-year phonogram term expired before the 2013 extension. title: Pomp and Circumstance, Op. 39
work.title: Pomp and Circumstance
work.version.value: Orchestral version
work.version.note: The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.
performers.note: The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.
session.date.note: Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.
session.place.note: Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.
carrier.label.note: The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.
carrier.catalogue.note: Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.
transfer.credits.value: George Blood, L.P.; Phoebe Pugh, transfer
transfer.credits.note: The item identifies the digitisation facility and user_transferred field; these are transfer credits, not original session personnel.
transfer.date.note: The November 2023 upload does not establish the transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.8 mil truncated-conical stylus transfer; equalised with turnover 250 and rolloff 0; MP3 derivative
transfer.processing.note: The original FLAC’s embedded comment identifies the selected stylus and equalisation. The site uses the supplied preferred MP3 without joining or changing the audio.

rights.composition.note: Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927
rights.recording.note: Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. The Naxos booklet is used only as documentary evidence: its commercial restoration is not the selected audio.

title: Requiem, Op. 48
work.title: Requiem
work.version.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
work.version.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.
performers.value: [{"name":"Chorale Philippe Caillard","role":"chorus"},{"name":"Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo","role":"orchestra"},{"name":"Louis Frémaux","role":"conductor"},{"name":"Henri Carol","role":"organ"}]
performers.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.
session.date.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.
session.place.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
session.place.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
carrier.label.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.
carrier.catalogue.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.27 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 3 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).
transfer.credits.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.
transfer.date.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.44 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

title: Requiem, Op. 48
work.title: Requiem
work.version.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
work.version.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.
performers.value: [{"name":"Bernard Kruysen","role":"baritone"},{"name":"Chorale Philippe Caillard","role":"chorus"},{"name":"Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo","role":"orchestra"},{"name":"Louis Frémaux","role":"conductor"},{"name":"Henri Carol","role":"organ"}]
performers.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; Kruysen is the baritone soloist here (the sleeve credits “Bernard Kruysen, baryton”). Denis Thilliez has no part in this movement.
session.date.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.
session.place.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
session.place.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
carrier.label.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.
carrier.catalogue.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.44 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 2 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).
transfer.credits.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.
transfer.date.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.49 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

rights.composition.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
rights.composition.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.
rights.recording.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
rights.recording.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

performers.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording. The sleeve credits “Denis Thilliez, soprano garçon” as the only soprano soloist, and the Pie Jesu is the Requiem’s only soprano solo, so his part here is inferred rather than stated. title: Rhapsody in Blue
work.title: Rhapsody in Blue
work.version.value: Gershwin’s 1924 acoustic recording with Paul Whiteman’s band, in Ferde Grofé’s original jazz-band orchestration; abridged for two sides of Victor 55225
work.version.note: The selected source supplies a single, already-joined MP3 of both parts. Contrapunctus has not joined separate 78 sides. It is the complete issued abridgement, not an uncut performance of the score. Schiff’s Table 1 distinguishes these recording cuts from the cuts in the solo-piano arrangement. The three listening sections group the introduction, the faster dances, and the broad melody with its piano continuation and finale; their starts are passage-level editorial estimates, without bar alignment or aural review. The source does not identify the score or parts used at the session.
performers.value: [{"name":"George Gershwin","role":"piano"},{"name":"Paul Whiteman Concert Orchestra","role":"jazz band"},{"name":"Paul Whiteman","role":"conductor"}]
performers.note: The Library of Congress credits Gershwin as pianist and Whiteman as leader. Farrington’s essay additionally identifies Ross Gorman’s clarinet and Henry Busse’s trumpet. No complete session personnel list is asserted.
session.date.note: Recording date of both Victor sides; separate from the September release and the modern upload.
session.place.note: City is documented. A particular Victor studio address or room has not been established.
carrier.label.note: Original commercial issue. The image accompanying the selected transfer shows the blue Victor label, but its relationship to the physical copy digitised is unknown.
carrier.catalogue.note: Two sides of one 12-inch disc. Bolig dates publication to 5 September 1924; the same day’s Chicago Tribune advertisement lists both parts under 55225, price $1.50, beneath the heading ‘Out today’.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Part 1: C-30174, take 1; Part 2: C-30173, take 2
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The side-specific Library of Congress catalogue records and Bolig’s discography agree on these matrix/take assignments, which are preferred here. work.title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D
work.version.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (11 of the three suites), the 50 bars and the closing string-only Adagio match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
work.version.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The numbering 11–15 for this suite follows the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) and IMSLP; other editions may agree. The recording plays the closing Adagio (bars 48–50, strings only): about six soft chord attacks, roughly three seconds apart, follow the last tutti chord, and the official video shows the violins playing at about 1:46–2:00. The stretch is identified from the score, the six level peaks and the video, not by listening; whether anything else is audible after the last chord has not been checked by ear.

title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D, HWV 349
work.title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D
work.version.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (15 of the three suites) and the structure heard (a four-bar and an eight-bar strain, each repeated, the whole air played three times) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text and its instruction “This Air to be played 3 times over”; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
work.version.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured pauses and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 12 bars with repeat signs and the instruction on p. 53; IMSLP lists the movement as 12 bars played three times (36). The higher level of the third pass is a feature of this performance: the printed notes are the same for all three.
performers.value: [{"name":"Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band","role":"orchestra"},{"name":"Major Michelle A. Rakers","role":"conductor"}]
performers.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The wide shot in this video’s thumbnail shows a harpsichord at stage left, strings with a double bass and a bassoon; a trumpet is visible in the Hornpipe video, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each of the three passes is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 0:34, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

work.title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D
work.version.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (12 of the three suites) and the structure heard (39-bar first section played twice, 35-bar middle section, da capo to the Fine at bar 39 without the repeat) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
work.version.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured level curve and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints a repeat sign after bar 39, the Fine mark at bar 39, and da capo at bar 74. IMSLP’s tally of 74 bars (133 with da capo) does not agree with that reading (74 plus 39 bars of da capo gives 113) and is not used.

work.version.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (14 of the three suites) and the structure heard (first strain of 19 bars played twice, second strain of 15 bars without brass, da capo to the fermata chord) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
work.version.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured silences and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 34 bars with a fermata, the mark Fine and a repeat sign at bar 19 and da capo at bar 34; IMSLP’s tally of 34 bars (53 with da capo) agrees.

title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D, HWV 349
work.title: Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D
work.version.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (13 of the three suites) and the strains heard (a first strain of 8 bars and a second of 16, each played twice) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text. The recording then plays all 24 bars once more without repeats, which that edition does not print; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
work.version.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) prints 24 bars with a repeat sign after bar 8 and after bar 24 and no da capo; the second statement follows from the measured pauses (about 54 s for 24 bars at the first statement’s pace) and is a feature of this performance. Commons and the candidate list place this movement fifth in the suite; the edition numbers it third (13), and Arnold’s 1788 score prints it last, headed Coro.
performers.value: [{"name":"Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band","role":"orchestra"},{"name":"Major Michelle A. Rakers","role":"conductor"}]
performers.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The video’s closing frames show the whole orchestra standing; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each statement is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 1:05, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.
session.date.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. This Minuet is the last item of the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

work.title: Symphony No. 94 in G major “Surprise”
work.version.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.
session.date.value: 22 and 24 April 1929: the first side on 22 April, the second side on 24 April
session.date.note: Young’s discography lists the first side (CVE-48983-2) with the 22 April 1929 session and the second side (CVE-48986-2) with a later recording date of 24 April 1929 for the published retaken side. DAHR’s list for 24 April 1929 includes CVE-48986 and Bolig gives take 2 for the second side. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.
session.place.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
session.place.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.
carrier.catalogue.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side 1: CVE-48983, take 2 (22 April 1929); side 2: CVE-48986, take 2 (24 April 1929)
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Young gives CVE-48983-2 and CVE-48986-2 as the issued takes of the first movement’s two sides. Bolig independently gives CVE-48986 take 2 for part 2. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

transfer.date.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.
transfer.processing.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
transfer.processing.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

title: Psalm 24 — La terre appartient à l’Éternel
work.title: Psalm 24 — La terre appartient à l’Éternel
work.version.value: Complete French psalm setting with tenor solo, mixed chorus, brass, timpani, harp and organ; no orchestral strings or woodwinds.
work.version.note: The precise performing edition is unidentified. The viewed nomenclature labels Harpe in the singular, while some work lists say two harps; no performer count is invented. Optional opening horn reinforcement is not asserted as heard.

work.version.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.
performers.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.
session.date.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).
session.place.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.
carrier.label.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number is given for the source of this file.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No acetate matrix, side or take numbers appear in the sources consulted; this is not a claim that they cannot be recovered.
transfer.credits.note: The item names an uploader account but no transfer or restoration engineer; an uploader is not automatically a transfer engineer.
transfer.date.note: The item’s added and public dates (2 July 2022) are upload dates, not transfer dates.
transfer.processing.value: Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (170 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed.
transfer.processing.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation. The Internet Archive item also carries a separate 15-second clip (track 07, “Zwischenruf 6. Satz at 19 min 30 sec (3x)”) in which the uploader isolated an audience interjection that he places at about 19 min 30 s of this movement; the clip is not part of this recording and the words shouted are the uploader’s uncertain hearing.
digital.format: VBR MP3 (170 kbps) derivative supplied by the Internet Archive; original upload WAV
rights.composition.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
rights.composition.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.
rights.recording.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
rights.recording.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

work.title: Rückert-Lieder
work.movement: Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen — concert-band arrangement
work.version.value: Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified
work.version.note: Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467
work.title: Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major
work.version.note: The exact performing edition is not identified. Bolig explicitly credits Artur Schnabel with the first-movement cadenza; the consulted public-domain score marks the cadenza slot but does not contain his notes. The Archive description says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current file attribution follows that corrected record, not the superseded review. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.
performers.note: The Archive description, photographed LP sleeve and orchestra discography agree. Bolig and the Schnabel chronology identify a Bechstein piano. The later sleeve uses Sargent’s title Sir; that is not treated as evidence of his title at the 1937 session.
session.date.note: LSO session 0158 distinguishes K. 467, recorded on 12 January, from K. 459, recorded on 9 and 12 January. The date is independently stated in the Archive description and the side-level discographies.
session.place.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1. The recording venue is not inferred merely from the orchestra’s name.
carrier.label.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
carrier.label.note: This is the documented mono LP used for Bob Varney’s transfer, not the original shellac carrier. The original recording was issued by His Master’s Voice.
carrier.catalogue.note: The photographed sleeve prints COLH 67 and pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. LSO session 0158 dates COLH67 to November 1959 and the original K. 467 issue, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. This movement originally occupied DB3099 and DB3100.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4604-1, 2EA 4605-1, 2EA 4606-1 and 2EA 4607-2A; first movement parts 1–4 on HMV DB3099–3100.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Those issued matrix/take numbers are explicitly documented by Bolig and the Schnabel chronology. Their survival in this particular Angel LP transfer is inferred, not established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No original side-join timestamps are assigned. A targeted DAHR search produced no directly usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.
transfer.credits.value: Bob Varney
transfer.credits.note: The source expressly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; this credit is not inferred from the uploader account.
transfer.date.note: The item was added on 19 April 2010, and the current MP3 has a later file timestamp following the documented correction. Neither is an identified analogue-to-digital transfer date.
transfer.processing.note: The source identifies a mono LP transfer but gives no cartridge, equalisation, noise-reduction, editing or speed-correction procedure. Internet Archive labels the uploaded file VBR MP3 and original; ‘original’ here means the uploaded file, not an original session master.
digital.format: Internet Archive original-upload VBR MP3; documented source carrier: mono LP. Duration is the analysed file length, rounded to one decimal place.
rights.composition.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; Schnabel’s own cadenza is also beyond that term.
rights.composition.note: Mozart died in 1791; the consulted score derives from the 1878 Breitkopf edition. Schnabel died in 1951, giving an ordinary life-plus-70 expiry at the end of 2021 for his authorship. This is a territorial term calculation, not clearance of every modern edition or a claim about US cadenza publication history.
rights.recording.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
rights.recording.note: The LSO discography documents publication before 1963, independently of the 1937 session date. The ordinary EU 50-year sound-recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This package uses that territorial basis only. US public-domain status is not established: this is not a recording first published by 1925. The Archive uploader links http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/, but that declaration does not independently establish authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The linked legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.version.value: Traditional Süssmayr Communio, adapting Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
work.version.note: The NMA labels the movement Süssmayr after Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie. This is not an independently completed final movement in Mozart’s surviving manuscript. Süssmayr’s 1800 letter explains reuse of the Kyrie fugue; Constanze’s reported instruction from Mozart is testimony, not independent verification of a complete plan. File duration includes a retained live-recording tail after the estimated musical close.
performers.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.
session.date.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.
session.place.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
session.place.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.
carrier.label.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number is attached to the transferred source. Cetra LO516, Nuova Era 2209, Seven Seas K30Y307 and Orfeo C430961B are documented release leads only. The festival catalogue dates Orfeo C 430 961 B to 1996; that is not evidence of first release or byte provenance.

work.title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.version.value: Traditional Mozart–Süssmayr completion, Dies irae; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
work.version.note: Mozart left the vocal and bass framework and some instrumental indications; the traditional completed orchestration is used as the reference. The recording sources do not name a printed edition. The NMA preface quotes Walter’s policy of cutting some trombone doublings, but does not map it to this 1956 performance. The complete movement includes its orchestral postlude.

work.title: Requiem in D minor, K. 626
work.version.value: Mozart’s completed Introitus, within the traditional Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem; performing edition unidentified.
work.version.note: The NMA distinguishes the Introitus, fully orchestrated by Mozart, from the incomplete later movements. The file contains this complete opening movement, stopping before the Kyrie. The traditional version is an identification from the repertory and score comparison, not an edition named by the upload. Walter’s precise instrumental alterations are unestablished.
performers.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

work.version.value: Traditional Süssmayr completion of Mozart’s Lacrimosa; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
work.version.note: Mozart’s surviving draft breaks off after bar 8. The conventional completion continues the movement and closes with the short Amen, rather than a later reconstructed Amen fugue. work.version.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
work.version.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

work.version.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
work.version.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

work.version.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
work.version.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

title: Douce dame jolie / L’espoir que j’ai
movement: Machaut and Janequin · Weckerlin arrangements · complete Victor side
work.title: Douce dame jolie / L’espoir que j’ai
work.movement: Complete paired Victor side: Machaut and Janequin in later arrangements
work.version.value: Two songs from J.-B. Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé, volume I, performed with harp and lute
work.version.note: The label numbers Machaut’s Douce dame jolie first and Janequin’s L’espoir que j’ai second; DAHR quotes the collection title and volume from Victor’s ledgers. BnF describes the published collection as voice with piano, so the precise harp-and-lute adaptation is not established from that score.
work.date.value: Fourteenth- and sixteenth-century songs; nineteenth-century published arrangement collection
work.date.note: The label prints 1350 A.D. and 1530 A.D. as historical song dates; these are retained only as label assertions, not verified composition dates. BnF dates volume I to 1853–1857.
work.completeness.value: Entire published two-song acoustic side; not a complete original Machaut virelai
work.completeness.note: No digital mid-phrase extract is made. Original stanza completeness and the exact boundary between the two arranged songs are unestablished; the side remains one authored section.
performers.note: DAHR identifies Raymond Dixon as Murphy’s pseudonym, not a second singer. Di Stefano is credited for takes 3–4; Francis J. Lapitino belongs only to discarded takes 1–2 and is not credited on this issued take.
session.date.note: Take 4 was made on 17 March 1915. The earlier matrix date 14 January 1915 refers to destroyed takes 1–2, not the recording streamed here.
session.place.value: New York, New York, United States
session.place.note: DAHR specifies New York for takes 3–4. Camden belongs to the January takes and is not substituted for this session; the studio address is unknown.
carrier.label.value: Victor Talking Machine Company; blue label
carrier.label.note: The viewed label names Victor and Lambert Murphy and specifies tenor with harp and lute, in French.
carrier.catalogue.note: The side suffix B is visible on the label. LOC and DAHR identify the 10-inch carrier.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR marks take 4 as Master and links the same audio. Matrix/take identification comes from discographic records, not from claiming to read an illegible run-out inscription.
carrier.publication.note: Bolig’s entry 45083 gives May-16 as release date. This corrects the Archive mirror’s claim of first publication in 1915, which conflates release with the session year.
transfer.credits.value: Source disc: UCSB Davidson Library, Department of Special Collections; National Jukebox digital access; Hessel Digital Library mirror
transfer.credits.note: LOC identifies the source collection. The mirror credits digitisation to the Library of Congress Packard Campus; DAHR also describes the audio as from the UCSB Library. No individual transfer engineer is established.
transfer.date.note: The original disc-transfer date is unknown. The Archive mirror states LOC retrieval on 30 September 2026 and repository publication on 10 October 2026; neither is the 1915 session or 1916 release.
transfer.processing.value: Archive describes its MP3 as a bit-exact copy of the LOC-served MP3, with no processing
transfer.processing.note: This records the mirror’s provenance statement, not an independently performed checksum comparison. Original stylus, speed correction, equalisation and noise-reduction settings are unknown. No additional audio cut is made.
digital.format: MP3 mirror of the complete National Jukebox side
rights.composition.value: Historical songs and Weckerlin collection are outside ordinary composition copyright terms
rights.composition.note: BnF gives Weckerlin’s dates 1821–1910 and the collection’s publication in 1853–1857. The exact person responsible for adapting its piano accompaniment to harp and lute is not established. Recording admission rests independently on the documented pre-cutoff publication.
rights.recording.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: published May 1916
rights.recording.note: Victor 45083’s documented 1916 publication precedes the project’s 1925 cutoff. source.rights uses us-published-before-cutoff with published 1916. The Archive Public Domain Mark is corroborative, not the sole basis; its 1915 first-publication claim and simplified statutory explanation are not repeated. This is a US basis, not a claim of worldwide clearance.
rights.creditLine: Machaut, Douce dame jolie, and Janequin, L’espoir que j’ai, from Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé; Lambert Murphy, tenor, Stefano Di Stefano, harp, William Carlino, lute. Recorded New York, 17 March 1915; Victor 45083-B, matrix B-15595, take 4; released May 1916. Source disc UCSB; Library of Congress, National Jukebox; Hessel Digital Library mirror on Internet Archive. US public-domain recording.

work.title: Quel augellin che canta
work.version.value: Five-part unaccompanied vocal setting, SSATB

work.publication.note: Publication date, not a guessed composition year.

title: Sicut lilium inter spinas
work.title: Sicut lilium inter spinas
work.version.value: Unaccompanied motet for cantus, altus, tenor, second tenor and bassus
work.version.note: The five-part score is the motet, not the Mass of the same name. The album lists the motet as track 1 and the Mass movements separately. The choir’s exact performing edition and pitch are not identified.
work.publication.note: 1569 is publication, not an asserted exact composition year. Suggestions that it may be an early work are not converted into a date.
work.text.value: Song of Songs, beginning with the lily among thorns comparison, followed by Alleluia
work.text.note: The text is described as a whole; no line is assigned an exact timestamp without alignment.
work.completeness.note: No Mass movement is appended, and no editorial audio excerpt is made.
work.scoreEdition.value: Theodor de Witt, Palestrina’s Werke, volume I, Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1862, plate 10414
work.scoreEdition.note: Public-domain edition. Motet No. 21 spans printed pp. 90–94, PDF pp. 104–108; those pages were opened and viewed, including the final cadence on p. 94.
performers.note: These are credits for the nominated recording, not the separate Hyperion performances consulted for programme notes. Individual singers and choir size are not identified.
session.date.note: FMA describes a live minidisc recording and gives the album date as 29 July 2007. The choir’s own archive documents the matching Renaissance Influences programme on that date. Their conjunction supports a probable session date, but the track description does not explicitly identify the session day. The FMA track’s 20 August 2010 is its online release.
session.place.value: Sacred Heart Cathedral, Hill Street, Wellington, New Zealand
session.place.note: The official archive supplies the venue for the matching 29 July 2007 concert. The link between that concert and the recording is inferred from title, director, programme and album date, not stated in the track description.
carrier.label.note: No original recording label or commercial imprint is named; Free Music Archive is the distribution platform.
carrier.catalogue.note: The album title and track number are known, but no release catalogue number is supplied.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The source describes a live minidisc recording, not a pressed disc matrix; no session take number is supplied.

title: Barcarolle, Op. 10 No. 3
work.title: Barcarolle
work.version.value: Solo piano, performed by the composer
work.version.note: No performing score edition is identified, and the printed text is not asserted to match the performance.
session.date.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register and the Library of Congress bulletin give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.
session.place.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The Library of Congress bulletin names Edison Studios, New York. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.
carrier.label.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.
carrier.catalogue.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82202 (10-inch double-faced; Barcarolle on side L, Chopin’s Valse in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3, on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
carrier.catalogue.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Library of Congress bulletin; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by Densmore (February 1921) and by the Library of Congress ([1921]) and is not followed for the release date; either year is before 1926.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The RCA register names Edison 6743-C for CD 10, track 16, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).
transfer.credits.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
transfer.credits.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.
transfer.date.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
transfer.processing.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.
digital.format: VBR MP3 access derivative; the uploaded source is a WAV taken from a 1992 CD reissue of an acoustic disc
rights.composition.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.
rights.recording.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82202, released February 1921).
rights.recording.note: Densmore’s Edison list gives a February 1921 release for 82202, and the Library of Congress Cataloging Service Bulletin 61 catalogues the disc as Edison [1921]; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. This file is the complete transfer of the slow movement’s first original side, part 4 of the concerto’s disc sequence. It omits the subsequent sides, including the later central section, cadenza and return; no sides have been joined.

session.date.note: DAHR identifies take 1 as the issued master. The Archive’s November 1929 date describes the HMV issue, not the recording session.
session.place.note: The matrix’s Take Date and Place table names the Academy of Music. Camden in the issue’s MARC publisher imprint is not adopted as a recording venue.
carrier.label.value: His Master’s Voice / The Gramophone Co. Ltd.
carrier.label.note: UK 12-inch 78-rpm pressing, manufactured at Hayes, Middlesex, England according to the label.
carrier.catalogue.note: The label marks the side No. 4 and 2nd Movement–Adagio sostenuto (1st Record). The other face contains the first movement’s third side. Internet Archive dates the HMV issue to November 1929; DAHR’s generated MARC imprint gives [1929].

carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR connects the master take to DB-1334 and distinguishes 2-05744 as a Gramophone face number. The Archive transcribes A48966 as another disc identifier; it is not treated as a separate performance or take.

transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.3-mil truncated-conical stylus transfer, equalised with turnover 500.0; 24-bit FLAC master and VBR MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The Archive documents four stylus transfers and identifies the chosen stylus in the preferred FLAC comment. Surface noise limits automatic onset and pitch-class estimates; these are not treated as counts of played notes or verified changes of key.
