title: Lilacs, Op. 21 No. 5 (composer’s piano transcription)
work.title: Lilacs (composer’s piano transcription)
work.version.value: Solo-piano transcription of the song Lilacs (1902), made by the composer in 1913
work.version.note: The RCA register labels the track “Transcription: Rachmaninoff”, DAHR catalogues it as piano solo and Sudbin dates the transcription to summer 1913. The performing edition, and whether the composer varied the printed text, are not identified.
session.date.note: DAHR’s approved take 9 is dated 27 December 1923; the Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date. Earlier takes from 1920, 1922 and October 1923 were not issued.
session.place.note: DAHR gives Camden, New Jersey for takes 8–9; the Church Building laboratory is named only for the first take of 1920.
carrier.label.note: Victor is the original label; the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.
carrier.catalogue.value: Victor 1051 (10-inch double-faced, coupled with Tchaikovsky’s Humoresque); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
carrier.catalogue.note: Victor 64906 was an earlier single-faced number marked not issued. The disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR names the matrix, takes and issues. The link between that take and this digital file rests on the RCA register (which names the matrix and take for the CD track) and the uploader’s CD identification; no waveform or run-out comparison with the disc was made.
transfer.credits.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
transfer.credits.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.
transfer.date.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
transfer.processing.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.
digital.format: VBR MP3 access derivative; the uploaded source is a WAV taken from a 1992 CD reissue of an acoustic disc
rights.composition.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition. The song text is Ekaterina Beketova’s and the transcription is the composer’s own.
rights.recording.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 1051, recorded 1923).
rights.recording.note: DAHR’s catalogue record for Victor 1051 gives a publication date of [1923], and an Internet Archive digitisation of Victrola 1051-A gives 1923; both are catalogue-derived years, not release days. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists “Lilacs (Rachmaninoff, Op. 21, No. 5)” on 1051, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

title: Polka de V.R. (Polka de W. R.)
work.title: Polka de V.R. (Polka de W. R.)
work.version.value: Composer’s arrangement for piano (1911) of Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka Lachtäubchen, Op. 303, as played by him
work.version.note: The printed title is Polka de W. R. (W. for Wassily, the composer’s father); the RCA set and the Archive file use V.R. Behr’s theme is transposed from F to A♭ with an added counter-melody and without Behr’s middle section. The score prints ossia alternatives, and the edition used by the composer for this recording is not identified.
session.date.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.
session.place.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.
carrier.label.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.
carrier.catalogue.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82187 (10-inch double-faced; Polka on side L, Prelude in C♯ minor on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
carrier.catalogue.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Florida Atlantic catalogue; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by the National Park Service and Densmore (December 1920) and is not followed for the release date; either proposed publication year predates 1926.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The RCA register names Edison 6744-B for CD 10, track 15, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

transfer.processing.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

title: Sérénade, Op. 3 No. 5
work.title: Sérénade
work.version.value: Original (1892) version of the Sérénade, as played by the composer in 1922; performing text not identified
work.version.note: Wikipedia’s list of the composer’s recordings labels the 4 November 1922 recording the 1892 version, and the 1940 revised version was published only in 1940 (Henle). IMSLP’s page says No. 5 was revised in 1922; the Henle report documents the revised text as Charles Foley’s 1940 edition, so that remark is not followed. Henle also states that the composer’s own recording diverges from the printed notation of the original version in many places. Henle does not identify which composer recording it means; the cited original score is therefore not assumed to be a literal transcript of the 1922 performance.
session.date.note: DAHR’s approved take 5 is dated 4 November 1922; takes 1–3 were made on 1 November. The Archive filename and the RCA register give the same date for the reissued track.
session.place.note: DAHR gives New York for every take; no studio is named.
carrier.label.note: Victor is the original label; the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.
carrier.catalogue.value: Victor 66129 (10-inch single-faced) and Victor 816 (10-inch double-faced, with Bizet’s Minuet); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
carrier.catalogue.note: The Victor numbers and the CD set are separately documented. The disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: DAHR names the matrix, takes and issues. The link between that take and this digital file rests on the RCA register (which names the matrix and take for the CD track) and the uploader’s CD identification; no waveform or run-out comparison with the disc was made.
transfer.credits.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
transfer.credits.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.
transfer.date.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
transfer.processing.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis.
digital.format: VBR MP3 access derivative; the uploaded source is a WAV taken from a 1992 CD reissue of an acoustic disc
rights.composition.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
rights.composition.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.
rights.recording.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 66129 and 816, recorded 1922).
rights.recording.note: DAHR’s catalogue records for Victor 66129 and 816 give a publication date of [1922], and an Internet Archive digitisation of Victrola 66129 gives 1922; both are catalogue-derived years, not release days. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists the Serenade (Op. 3, No. 5) coupled with the Minuet from L’Arlésienne, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

title: La Poule
work.title: La Poule
work.catalogue: Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin, G-major/minor suite
work.version.value: Solo piano performance of the harpsichord character piece
work.version.note: The hosted item is La Poule alone, not the whole suite. The collection is conventionally dated about 1728; this is an approximate publication date, not a documented composition day. Meyer’s performing edition, editorial interventions and repeat choices are unestablished. The reference score supplies the musical design, not evidence that Meyer used that edition.
performers.note: The recording is performed on piano; the harpsichord designation belongs to Rameau’s original work.
session.date.note: Commons’ Author field and the discography identify this two-day Rameau session. Neither allocates La Poule to one of the two days. The Commons Date and structured inception fields say 22 August 2019, matching the upload, not the performance.
session.place.note: The venue is stated in both opened recording sources; no session log or microphone layout is available.
carrier.label.note: The named source collection is the Médiathèque musicale Mahler’s fonds Discophiles Français.
carrier.catalogue.note: The paired catalogue reference identifies the Rameau programme; the individual disc and side used for this transfer are not allocated. The chronology identifies an LP issue, not a 78-rpm side.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take, pressing inscription or exact side allocation is established from the opened sources.
transfer.credits.note: The source collection and uploader Flopinot2012 are identified. Neither is automatically the transfer or restoration engineer; no such engineer is credited.
transfer.date.note: 22 August 2019 is the upload date. The transfer date is not supplied.
transfer.processing.note: FLAC upload and Commons MP3 derivative are documented, but restoration, equalisation, speed correction, editing and the transferred carrier’s physical condition are not. No quality claim is inferred from the lossless upload format.
digital.format: Wikimedia Commons MP3 derivative of FLAC; source credited to Médiathèque musicale Mahler, fonds Discophiles Français
rights.composition.value: Public-domain underlying composition
rights.composition.note: Commons applies PD-old-70-expired to the work; Rameau died in 1764. This is separate from copyright in the recorded performance or an unidentified edition.
rights.recording.value: Territorial — Commons PD-EU-audio sound-recording status
rights.recording.note: The sound-recording-specific PD-EU-audio tag is the programme’s acceptance basis. It states expiry of European performers’ and producers’ rights. US public-domain status is not established and is not asserted. The composition’s public-domain statement does not establish the recording’s US status, and the session date is not substituted for a proven first-publication date.

title: Four Last Songs
work.title: Four Last Songs
work.version.value: Complete song in the original scoring for soprano and orchestra, sung in German
work.version.note: The fourth song is separately banded on the LP and transferred as one complete track. The published score places the orchestral prelude on pp. 44–46, the vocal stanzas on pp. 46–54, and the postlude on pp. 54–55. Hall sections and musical cues use approximate score-proportion passage timings; no bar alignment or syllable-level timing is asserted. The edition of the orchestral parts used at the session is unknown.
performers.note: All three credits appear on the original side-one label. The consulted sources do not identify the individual orchestral soloists. This is the Ackermann recording, distinct from Schwarzkopf’s later recording with George Szell.
session.date.note: Warner’s reissue metadata, reproduced by Presto, dates the Four Last Songs to 25 September 1953 and the accompanying Capriccio scene to 26 September. Naxos gives 25–26 September for the songs. Month-level precision retains the date on which both accounts agree; the exact day and take of Im Abendrot remain unresolved.
session.place.note: The Warner track documentation names Watford Town Hall. The original Angel label states Recorded in England.
carrier.label.note: The source is an original Angel vinyl LP transfer, not the later Warner or Naxos digital remaster.
carrier.catalogue.note: Internet Archive catalogues this United States release as 1954. The booklet carries the 1954 copyright notice for Edward Cushing’s English translations.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side 1, band 4; printed side matrix XAX-380; label number 1-35084
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: XAX-380 and 1-35084 are visible on the side-one label; the track listing places Im Abendrot fourth on that side. No take number or pressing-specific runout suffix has been established.
transfer.credits.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation
transfer.credits.note: The institutional contributor is credited; no personal account identifier or additional restoration credit is reproduced.
transfer.date.note: The ripping_date field is 20210622081253. The sleeve scan is dated 31 May 2021; neither date is a recording-session or LP-publication date.
transfer.processing.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; whole-side 24-bit FLAC transfer and segmented VBR MP3 access derivative
transfer.processing.note: The playback chain is stated in the item metadata. The whole-side FLAC is marked Processed by SoX; the selected MP3 is derived through the item’s segment data. Equalisation settings, pitch adjustment, noise reduction and other restoration decisions are unknown.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of a vinyl LP transfer
rights.composition.value: Strauss’s music and Eichendorff’s German poem are public domain under ordinary EU life-plus-70 terms.
rights.composition.note: Strauss died in 1949 and Eichendorff in 1857. This assessment concerns Im Abendrot alone, not the three other songs’ Hermann Hesse texts. The score was first published in 1950 and remains identified by IMSLP as protected in the United States; no US composition clearance is asserted. The copyrighted English translation in the LP booklet is not reproduced.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public domain under the pre-1963 commercial-publication rule: Angel 35084 was published in 1954.
rights.recording.note: The documented 1954 lawful commercial issue predates the programme’s 1963 cutoff. Its former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013. This is a territorial term assessment, not a Creative Commons licence or a declaration of US or worldwide public-domain status. The transferred LP, not a modern commercial remaster, supplies the audio.
rights.creditLine: Richard Strauss, Four Last Songs: IV. Im Abendrot, text by Joseph von Eichendorff; Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, Philharmonia Orchestra, Otto Ackermann. Recorded September 1953, Watford Town Hall; Angel 35084 (1954); Internet Archive LP transfer. Territorial EU public-domain basis; US rights not cleared.

work.title: Guillaume Tell
work.version.value: Wind-ensemble transcription attributed to Wenzel Sedlak, adapted for the Marine Band’s Grand Scenes recording
work.version.note: The booklet explicitly says the attribution to Sedlak has not been conclusively proved. The overture comes from a fifteen-movement suite preserved at the Augustinian monastery in Brno. For this recording, the flute part was modified using Rossini’s orchestral part, two added trumpet parts were removed, and contrabassoon and string bass reinforced the bass. This is a small wind ensemble with double bass, not Rossini’s original full orchestral scoring.

title: Symphony No. 8 in B minor “Unfinished”, D. 759
work.title: Symphony No. 8 in B minor “Unfinished”
work.version.note: The performing edition and any cuts or retouchings by the conductor are not identified in the sources consulted.
session.date.note: Bolig dates all three sides of the first movement (CVE-29052, -29053 and -29054) to 28 April 1927. The Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days (28 and 30 April 1927) for the symphony as a whole.
session.place.value: Academy of Music, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
carrier.label.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.
carrier.catalogue.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29052, take 6; CVE-29053, take 6; CVE-29054, take 6
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Bolig and the Pristine producer’s note agree on the matrices and takes of the first movement. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.
transfer.credits.value: Bob Varney
transfer.credits.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.
transfer.processing.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 10:28; Pristine’s own restoration runs 10:33, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.
digital.format: Uploader-supplied MP3, classified as the original file by the Internet Archive (encoding history unknown); the Archive’s Ogg Vorbis file is its derivative

The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. work.title: String Quintet in C major
work.version.note: The performing edition is not identified. The Internet Archive file names print the posthumous opus number 163 for the work, which Schubert’s catalogue gives as D. 956.
performers.note: The Internet Archive item lists these five performers as creators; the Substack essay assigns the roles and calls the recording a Columbia release made at the Prades Festival. Which cellist plays the first cello part and which the second is not stated in any source consulted.
session.date.value: 1952 (the Casals Festival at Prades); one secondary source says July
session.date.note: The LP sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952; the Discogs master release and a 6moons review also say 1952. Only the Substack essay by John Buxton gives a month, July 1952, so the month is not treated as established, and the day is not stated.
session.place.value: Prades, France (Prades Festival); the venue within Prades is not identified
session.place.note: The sleeve notes say the recordings were made in Prades during the Casals Festival of 1952. Substack says the recording was made in Prades, France during the Prades Festival; Discogs and 6moons say it was recorded at the Prades Festival in 1952.
carrier.label.note: The label is the item’s publisher metadata and the title shown on its page.

carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side 1, second track of the LP (file 01.02 on the Internet Archive); matrix and take numbers are not established

transfer.credits.value: Internet Archive LP digitisation: ripped by an Internet Archive associate at the Cebu scanning centre (rip station archivelp-rip-cebu04); the cover was scanned and the item created by another associate
transfer.credits.note: The item metadata names a ripping operator and a ripping scanner, a scanning centre (cebu) and a separate scanning operator. The item is listed in several vinyl collections, including the Boston Public Library’s; which physical copy was digitised is not stated.
transfer.date.value: 4 January 2021 (the ripping date recorded in the item metadata)
transfer.date.note: The metadata gives ripping_date 20210104123741. The artwork scan date and public date are 24 November 2020 and the added date is 4 January 2021; these are separate events and the scan and upload dates are not transfer dates.
transfer.processing.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge, Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp and Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 interface; the Adagio file is an MP3 derivative of the side

rights.composition.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

title: Winterreise, D. 911
work.title: Winterreise
work.version.note: Utz measures this song at 4:11, the longest side of the set; no source consulted states the performing text or the key of the transfer. The transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.
performers.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.
session.date.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.
session.place.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.
carrier.label.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
carrier.label.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.
carrier.catalogue.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 386, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: CK 2956, take 1 (run-out “Ck 2956” with I); side No. 11 (label number 0942032); reverse side: Einsamkeit (matrix BK 2957-2). Disc 6 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.
transfer.credits.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.
transfer.processing.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (259.24 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (259.12 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

rights.composition.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
rights.recording.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

title: Winterreise, D. 911
work.title: Winterreise
work.version.note: Utz measures this song at 3:10 against a mean of 3:41 and describes a clear slowing in its second part. No source consulted states the key of the transfer; the transposition from the first edition and the absolute pitch are not established here.
performers.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.
session.date.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.
session.place.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.
carrier.label.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
carrier.label.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.
carrier.catalogue.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ER 276, and the Commons file name agrees. The Internet Archive text description of the disc reads “ER 376”, which the photograph does not support; the discrepancy is the uploader’s.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: BK 2969, take 1 (run-out “Bk 2969” with I); side No. 24 (label number 942922); reverse side: Die Nebensonnen (matrix CL 4401-1; pianist Lene Orthmann, 11 July 1928). Disc 12 of 12 of the set; 25 cm.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.
transfer.credits.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

The Commons duration (195.50 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (195.41 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

rights.recording.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
rights.recording.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

title: Symphony No. 5 in D minor, Op. 47
work.title: Symphony No. 5 in D minor
work.version.note: The work and movement are identified, but the exact performing edition is not. The historical score supports broad orchestration and formal observations, not a claim of bar-exact agreement with Rodzinski’s materials. The movement is the entire supplied source track; no local audio edit is made. The set’s finale has a separately disclosed reported cut.
performers.note: Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.
session.date.note: CiNii’s record for Westminster MVCW-18008 explicitly gives this range; the publisher independently lists the Rodzinski/Royal Philharmonic recording as 1954. Applying those reissue data to this differently credited LP is an inference. No original session ledger or precise movement-by-movement day has been located. 1956 is the selected LP’s publication year, not an invented session date.
session.place.note: Venue transcribed exactly from the reissue catalogue record. The original LP does not supply a venue. Its linkage to the selected LP is the same qualified inference as the session-date attribution; no more specific hall name is invented.
carrier.label.note: Original sleeve and labels; commercially issued Vinyl LP, Made in U.S.A. Sleeve ©1956 Westminster Recording Sales Corp.
carrier.catalogue.note: Both forms are visually present on the source object. These identify the selected 1956 issue, not an asserted first edition worldwide. The publisher lists an earlier 1955 Nixa issue of the attributed 1954 performance.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.value: Side 1: XTV 22720; movement 1 on that side
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: Label matrix is legible in the scan. Side 1 contains Moderato/Allegretto; side 2 contains Largo/Allegro non troppo. Take numbers and faint runout/stamper suffixes are unknown and are not guessed.
transfer.credits.value: Internet Archive
transfer.credits.note: The explicit ripping_operator field is credited, not the different uploader/cataloguing operator. A separately named restoration engineer and original recording engineer are unknown.
transfer.date.note: Derived from the explicit ripping_date field 20210915005548. This is not inferred from publicdate, scandate, addeddate or a later derivative timestamp; timezone is unspecified.
transfer.processing.value: LP transfer: Technics SL1200MK5 / Audio-Technica AT95e → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; ArchiveCD 2.2.57lp; source-side 24-bit FLAC and Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivatives
transfer.processing.note: Hardware lineage and ripping software are explicit metadata. Original side FLAC tags say Processed by SoX; exact filtering, declicking, gain, speed calibration and derivative segmentation parameters are unknown. The sleeve’s Panorthophonic tape-recording and RIAA-mastering statements concern the original production, not a modern restoration recipe. No local speed correction, normalization, splice or replacement audio was applied.
digital.format: Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivative of the LP side transfer; decoded duration rounded from cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-moderato.txt
rights.composition.value: Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis
rights.composition.note: Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
rights.recording.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

title: Finlandia, Op. 26
work.title: Finlandia
work.version.value: Abridged orchestral version; which passages are omitted is not documented
work.version.note: The abridgement is inferred from the file’s length, 4:06, against a typical performance of 7½–9 minutes (Wikipedia), and from the disc being a single 12-inch side. DAHR and the Internet Archive do not describe the cut, and neither names an edition or cut scheme. This dossier does not locate cut bars.
performers.note: DAHR gives Philadelphia Orchestra and Leopold Stokowski. The Internet Archive item credits “Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra”, a variant of the same ensemble’s name. DAHR’s instrumentation list (7 first violins, 5 second violins, 3 violas, 2 cellos, 4 basses, harp, 3 oboes, 3 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 trumpets, 3 trombones, 2 tubas, traps) comes from Victor ledgers for 15 March 1921 and is not confirmed for the issued take.
session.date.value: 18 April 1921 (issued take 4); earlier takes 1–2 on 15 March 1921
session.date.note: DAHR: takes 1 and 2 on 15 March 1921 and 3 on 18 April were destroyed; take 4 (18 April 1921) is the issued master. A bracketed [1921] is the date given for the issue on Victor 74698. Some listings give the earlier date for the first takes.
session.place.note: DAHR gives Camden, New Jersey for every take.
carrier.label.note: DAHR describes the object as Victor 74698, Red Seal 12-inch single-faced. Later issues on Victor 6366 and Gramophone Company DB-599 and 3-0662 are listed for the same matrix and take.
carrier.catalogue.note: The Internet Archive item also shows matrix and catalogue number 74698 and publisher “Victrola”.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The Internet Archive item shows 74698 as its matrix number; the Victor matrix is C-24988.
transfer.credits.value: [{"name":"George Blood, L.P.","role":"digitisation (scanning centre), Great 78 Project"}]
transfer.credits.note: The item metadata names George Blood, L.P. as scanning centre and credits Robert Boggs with metadata and transfer entry and Kevin Coupe with cleaning (as Internet Archive user fields).
transfer.date.note: The item’s public date is 19 March 2021; that is the upload date, not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four styli (3.8, 2.3, 2.8 and 3.3 mil truncated conical); the preferred version was selected by an engineer at George Blood and copied to the friendly file name
transfer.processing.note: The item’s notes say the record was acoustic and that the other side was “not completed due to physical condition of disc”. The MP3 used here is the Internet Archive derivative of the 24-bit FLAC; no further processing is disclosed.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of a 24-bit FLAC transfer
rights.composition.value: Sibelius died in 1957; in countries with a life-plus-70 term the composition remains in copyright until the end of 2027
rights.composition.note: Computed from the composer’s life dates, given in DAHR’s MARC record as 1865–1957. The composition’s status in other territories is not assessed. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording.
rights.recording.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: first published in 1921, before the 1926 cut-off.
rights.recording.note: DAHR records the issue on Victor 74698 as [1921]; the brackets mean the year was supplied by the cataloguer, and no month of issue is recorded. The take issued was made on 18 April 1921, so publication followed that date. The Internet Archive item date is also 1921. The item has no licence URL and no non-commercial restriction in its metadata.

title: Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 43
movement: Complete: I. Allegretto · II. Tempo andante, ma rubato · III. Vivacissimo · IV. Finale: Allegro moderato
work.title: Symphony No. 2 in D major
work.movement: Complete symphony in one file: I. Allegretto; II. Tempo andante, ma rubato; III. Vivacissimo; IV. Finale: Allegro moderato
work.version.value: The 1903 final version, as published by Fazer & Westerlund (the version in general use); the performing edition of this recording has not been checked against a score
work.version.note: The Sibelius Society gives the first version (premiere 8 March 1902) and the final version of 1903. The 1958 recording would normally use the published score; the Decca booklet lists Breitkopf & Härtel as publisher of the edition. No source states which version Monteux used, and no score alignment was made.
performers.note: Both the Internet Archive description and the Decca booklet credit the London Symphony Orchestra under Monteux. The leader and principals on this session are not documented here; the booklet’s essay says that Hugh Maguire joined as leader after the orchestra’s 1957 arrival of young players, without tying that to this date.
session.date.note: The Decca booklet gives Kingsway Hall, 18–20 June 1958, for the disc whose track list holds this symphony (PDF page 21, printed p. 40, beside the track list on PDF page 20, printed p. 39; the 24 and 25 June 1958 sessions marked with an asterisk are for Elgar’s Enigma Variations on the same disc). The Internet Archive description narrows the date to 20 June 1958 without a source. The identification rests on the layout of the booklet’s credits, which the author read as attaching to the disc listing Sibelius and Elgar; the measured movement lengths of this file (10:17, 14:36, 6:14 and 12:49) match the booklet’s track times (10:16, 14:36, 6:15, 12:49).
session.place.note: Both sources name Kingsway Hall.
carrier.label.value: RCA (US catalogue LSC 2342; UK catalogue SB 207); Decca reissue SDD 234 (September 1970)
carrier.label.note: The booklet’s “First released as” line names the catalogue numbers and months but not the label name for SB 207. The Internet Archive description says Decca–RCA. The author treats the first issue as RCA’s.
carrier.catalogue.note: The first issue was in October 1959 (LSC 2342) and May 1960 (SB 207); both dates are before 1963.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The booklet names no matrix, take or side numbers.
transfer.credits.note: The Internet Archive item was uploaded by a private account (subject tag “DWTKenInNY”); its description names no transfer engineer or source disc.
transfer.date.note: The item’s public date is 11 June 2023; that is an upload date, not a transfer date.
transfer.processing.value: A single VBR MP3 of the whole symphony; the uploader’s movement times are given in the description
transfer.processing.note: The Internet Archive derivative is a 78.7 MB VBR MP3 lasting 2,637 seconds. Whether it was sourced from an LP, CD or tape is not stated. No further processing is disclosed.
digital.format: VBR MP3 as uploaded to the Internet Archive; one 44-minute file for the whole symphony
rights.composition.value: Sibelius died in 1957, so the symphony (published 1903) is in copyright in countries with a life-plus-70 term, including the EU, until the end of 2027; IMSLP records it as public domain in the United States, Canada and life-plus-50 countries
rights.composition.note: The IMSLP work page carries a notice that the work is not in the public domain in life-plus-70 countries. The end date of 2027 is computed from Sibelius’s death in 1957, which the site’s Sibelius biography gives as 20 September 1957. This dossier does not claim the composition is out of copyright in the EU. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording, not the composition.
rights.recording.value: Rule 3 — EU public domain (territorial): first published before 1963 (RCA LSC 2342, October 1959; SB 207, May 1960).
rights.recording.note: Territorial only: the recording’s first publication in 1959–60 predates 1963, so its EU 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. The United States status of a 1958–59 sound recording is not established here. The Internet Archive item carries no licence URL; its metadata and description contain no non-commercial restriction. The item belongs to a general “folksoundomy” collection and was uploaded by a third party, not by the rights holder.

session.date.note: The original booklet states ‘Recorded June 1955 at La Scala with full orchestra and chorus.’ Youngrok Lee’s discography gives 6–7 June for these choruses, but the primary source supports month precision; a particular day and take for this track remain unidentified. session.place.note: The booklet explicitly names La Scala as the recording venue. A particular room, stage configuration or microphone layout is not established.

title: Six Pieces for Orchestra, Op. 6
work.title: Six Pieces for Orchestra
work.version.value: Original 1909 orchestral version
work.version.note: High Fidelity, September 1979, p. 129 explicitly identifies Craft's Columbia MS 6216 as the first version, distinguishing it from the 1928 revision in his separate complete-Webern set. The original score heads movement IV Langsam, marcia funebre; its central solo begins on alto flute, not the revision's clarinet. Section landmarks are broad score-proportion timings, without aural review.
performers.note: The original labels and contemporary review name the orchestra and conductor. The fourth piece uses wind instruments and percussion; individual players are not identified.
session.date.note: The sources establish the commercial issue but do not state this track's recording-session date. It is not assigned a date from Craft's separate 1950s complete-Webern project.
session.place.note: No recording venue is stated in the transfer metadata or original labels.
carrier.label.note: Original stereo LP imprint.
carrier.catalogue.note: Internet Archive dates this US stereo LP to 1960. Audio magazine reviewed MS 6216 in August 1961 and separately identified mono ML 5616. The rights assessment uses the conservative publication bound of 1961.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: The label lists Schoenberg as band 1 and Webern's six pieces as bands 2–7; No. 4 is therefore band 5. The matrix is printed on the label. No session take or stamper suffix is asserted.
transfer.credits.value: Internet Archive LP transfer
transfer.credits.note: The transfer institution is identified; no personal mastering credit is inferred from an operator account.
transfer.date.note: The ripping_date field is 20210730073437. The separate scan date is 9 July 2021.
transfer.processing.value: Technics SL1200MK5 with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; segmented VBR MP3 derivative
transfer.processing.note: The item documents the playback chain and derives tracks from a 24-bit FLAC side transfer. Equalisation settings, noise reduction and pitch correction are not established.
digital.format: VBR MP3 derivative of a stereo vinyl LP transfer
rights.composition.value: Underlying Webern composition is out of copyright under ordinary life-plus-70 terms.
rights.composition.note: Webern died in 1945. The original version was first published in 1913. This assessment concerns the composition in life-plus-70 territories, not every edition or jurisdiction; copyright in the cited 1961 score edition is separate and no worldwide clearance is asserted for that printed score.
rights.recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: commercial publication no later than 1961, before 1963.
rights.recording.note: Audio's August 1961 review establishes commercial availability of the exact LP. The Archive's 1960 date may identify an earlier issue; the conservative 1961 bound is sufficient for the project's former 50-year phonogram-term rule. This is not a Creative Commons licence; US recording status is not established.
